title: Sow in tears (Psalm 126)
hookLine: sung before grace on Shabbat: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy"
carry: sow in tears, reap in joy

cards: Thump, thump, thump. Hands on the tablecloth, keeping time. It's Shabbat or a festival, the long meal is over, plates pushed back, a few crumbs of challah left, kids getting restless.
Before the grace after meals, someone starts a song and the whole table joins in, often loudly. Shir ha-ma'alot: a Song of Ascents. In many families it's the sound of a full, happy table.
And right in the middle of it are the words: sow in tears.

teach.b: Psalm one twenty-six remembers a homecoming. When the Lord brought the exiles back to Zion, it says, we were like people dreaming. Our mouths filled with laughter, our tongues with song.

Even the nations said: God has done great things for them. Some readers hear it as the other side of Psalm one thirty-seven: the ones who wept by the rivers of Babylon come home, and it feels too good to be real.
In many Ashkenazi homes the two even share the table: one thirty-seven before grace on weekdays, one twenty-six on Shabbat.

Then a prayer: bring back the rest of us, like streams in the Negev, the southern desert, where dry riverbeds suddenly flood after rain. And then the farming picture: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy."

teach.h: SEED YOU CHOOSE NOT TO EAT.
teach.b: A farmer walks out weeping, carrying a bag of seed, and comes home with joy, carrying sheaves. Why weep while sowing? One common reading: in a hard year, seed is food a family chooses not to eat.
It goes into the ground on a hope, with grief and trust at the same time. The dreaming line has a story attached.
The Talmud says it puzzled Honi, the circle-drawer from weeks ago: how could seventy years of exile pass like a dream?
His answer began with a man planting a carob tree for his descendants, a tree whose fruit the planter would never eat.

teach.h: SOW IN TEARS, REAP IN JOY.
teach.b: That's sowing in tears. So at a full Shabbat table, the song is about tears, because the joy at the table grew from seeds someone once sowed, crying.

how: On Shabbat and festivals, many families sing Psalm 126, Shir ha-ma'alot, before Grace after Meals, often to lively tunes that everyone at the table knows.

o: a lullaby sung to children at bedtime
the blessing said over bread at a meal
a Song of Ascents, sung before grace

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: seed you choose not to eat

s: Psalm 126 is sung at the table before grace on Shabbat and festivals
often loudly, sometimes with the table as a drum.
the psalm is only about sadness
it's a homecoming song: laughter, song, and joy at the harvest.
Psalm 126 and Psalm 137 can share the same table
in many Ashkenazi homes, 137 comes before grace on weekdays and 126 on Shabbat and festivals.

games.q: it's a hard year. you have one bag of seed, and you're hungry. what does the farmer in Psalm 126 do?
o: sow it in tears, trusting in a harvest.
games.why: he goes out weeping, carrying seed, and comes home with joy, carrying sheaves. they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.

practice: Think of something hard you're doing whose fruit you can't see yet: raising a child, healing, learning, saving, rebuilding something broken.
Picture it as a seed in the ground and say, inside, what you hope it grows into; if you have a seed, a cutting or a bulb at hand, you can plant it with that hope. If you pray, ask for the harvest.

wordCard.voice: Shir ha-ma'alot. A Song of Ascents, sung before grace on Shabbat: the exiles came home like dreamers, and they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
